title: The railroad town that became the Sunset Strip
lede: West Hollywood began as Sherman, a yard town for Moses Sherman's electric railway. Because it stayed outside the Los Angeles city limits, its stretch of Sunset Boulevard became the Sunset Strip, home to nightclubs beyond the reach of the city's police, then to rock clubs, and finally to a city of its own, incorporated in 1984.
tl: The town of Sherman grows around the rail yards of Moses Sherman's Los Angeles Pacific Railroad.
Architect Rudolph Schindler builds his concrete-and-glass house on Kings Road.

The Pacific Design Center, the Blue Whale, opens.

p: The flats along Santa Monica Boulevard grew up as Sherman, where the Los Angeles Pacific Railroad kept its yards and shops. As Hollywood became famous, the town traded its name for West Hollywood in 1925. Its streets of bungalows and courtyard apartments date largely from those years.

fact: of Sunset Boulevard on the Strip
p: Because West Hollywood was unincorporated county land, the curving stretch of Sunset between Hollywood and Beverly Hills fell outside the Los Angeles Police Department's reach. In the 1930s and 1940s that made it the place for glamorous nightclubs like the Trocadero, Ciro's and the Mocambo, where studio stars were photographed every night. The Chateau Marmont, opened in 1929, became the hideaway hotel above it all.

ch.h: From the Whisky to a city
p: In the 1960s the supper clubs gave way to rock clubs. The Whisky a Go Go opened in 1964, and the Strip became a launching pad for bands from the Doors on. In 1966 crowds of young people protesting a curfew clashed with police, an episode remembered as the Sunset Strip riots. Residents voted to incorporate in 1984, and West Hollywood has since become one of the densest and most walkable cities in the county, anchored by the bright blue and green glass of the Pacific Design Center.
